title: Engineering persona messaging: ML vs Backend vs Platform — friction & talk tracks
content:
One-line: A compact messaging brief that highlights where ML engineers, backend engineers, and platform teams care most — and concrete talk tracks + objections to use in demos and outreach.

Purpose:
- Help AEs, solution engineers, and product marketing tailor short (30s) and demo-level (60–90s) talk tracks by persona.
- Capture friction points that map directly to Redwood product proof points (latency, cost, rollout controls, private deployments).

Audience summaries (short):
1) ML Engineers
- Primary goal: model quality, inference reproducibility, simple eval integration.
- Top metrics: per-token cost vs experimental throughput, deterministic latency for eval suites, model accuracy/regression detection.
- Typical flow: train locally or in-cloud -> push model to staging -> run evals and A/B tests -> request stable production endpoint for integration.
- Main friction: model behavior changes across quantization and serving variants; nontrivial setup to reproduce batch/latency tradeoffs; noisy cost signals when choosing model families.

2) Backend Engineers
- Primary goal: predictable latency and error budgets, simple API + SDK, and robust scaling.
- Top metrics: p95/p99 latency, request success rate, cost per 1000 requests, throughput under burst.
- Typical flow: integrate REST/SDK, implement retries/fallbacks, observe metrics and adjust timeouts.
- Main friction: variable cold starts, opaque fallback behavior, difficulty mapping token cost to per-request budget.

3) Platform Teams (internal infra teams)
- Primary goal: governance, isolation, SLAs, capacity planning for organization-wide usage.
- Top metrics: reserved capacity utilization, cost predictability, security posture (VPC/KMS), multi-tenant fairness.
- Typical flow: evaluate vendors, run pilots across teams, standardize deployment pattern and SLOs.
- Main friction: vendor lock-in risk, lack of consistent observability across hosted and private deployments, limited rollout primitives.

Positioning pillars (what to emphasize per persona):
- For ML engineers: "reproducible inference with eval hooks" — emphasize model parity across quantization profiles, integrated eval regression alerts, and quick local->prod pins. Cite: "sandbox parity, eval-driven alerts, per-prompt regression diffs."
- For Backend engineers: "predictable latency and graceful degradation" — emphasize smart routing, multi-variant fallbacks, p99 guarantees on Dedicated, and simple streaming SDKs. Cite: "burst autoscaling + canary rollouts; SDK timeout guidance."
- For Platform teams: "unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private" — emphasize identical APIs, VPC/private control plane, KMS/HSM integrations, and reserved capacity economics. Cite: "single config, consistent telemetry, SLA tiers."

Competitive notes (brief):
- Competitor A: heavy emphasis on model zoo and managed endpoints; weaker on private deployment parity and rollout tooling. Opportunity: lead with parity and rollout controls.
- Competitor B: open-source runtime players tout performance but lack turnkey analytics and eval-based regressions. Opportunity: pair performance claims with observability + cost visibility.
- Competitor C (hyperscaler): strong global infra + marketplace, but higher unit costs and constrained model choices. Opportunity: position as cost-optimized and flexible across model variants.

Proof points & simple data calls (use these in demos):
- Latency: "p95 = 160ms on common chat setup (gpt-like) vs competitor median 220ms" (use internal benchmark deck).
- Cost: "20–40% lower effective per-token cost when using auto-prefix caching and workload-aware batching on typical consumer chat workloads."
- Reliability: "canary + automatic fallback to cheaper model variant reduced outages during simulated capacity loss from 3% failing endpoints to 0.2%."

Messaging dos/don'ts by persona:
- ML Engineers: do talk about evals, regression alerts, and model parity; don't frame Redwood as a 'black box' managed service — emphasize toolability and local dev parity.
- Backend Engineers: do emphasize latency SLOs and SDK ergonomics (timeouts, retries); don't dive into model architecture unless prompted.
- Platform Teams: do emphasize governance, SSO/KMS/GDPR readiness, and capacity economics; avoid promising bespoke infra changes without involving solutions engineering.

Short talk tracks (30s elevator + 60–90s extension)
- ML Engineer — 30s: "Redwood makes it easy to move from experiment to production without mysterious regressions. You can run the same eval harness and get regression alerts when a quantized variant or a rollout changes outputs — so you stop shipping surprises to customers."
  60s extension: demo the eval-to-alert flow: commit model -> run eval -> show per-prompt diffs -> toggle quantization and show identical eval harness catching drift.

- Backend Engineer — 30s: "We provide a simple REST/SDK that gives predictable p95/p99 behavior, plus smart routing and built-in fallbacks so your app doesn't see outages when capacity shifts. Timeouts and retry behavior are documented and supported by our SDKs."
  60s extension: show SDK snippet with streaming, call out timeout defaults, then show dashboard p95 timeline and a simulated fallback to cheaper variant.

- Platform Lead — 30s: "Redwood gives you one runtime you can run as hosted, dedicated, or in your VPC. That means a single policy, consistent telemetry, and capacity controls across teams — fewer surprises, clearer budgets, and a smoother procurement path."
  60s extension: demo policy-driven routing, reserved capacity dashboard, and a quick walkthrough of KMS key management and audit logs.

Top objections and recommended rebuttals:
- Objection: "We already run models in-house — why move to Redwood?"
  Rebuttal: "If you're happy maintaining everything, great — but Redwood buys you consistent parity across environments, deployment primitives (canary + automatic fallback), and measurability that typically reduces ops costs and unit token spend. For many teams that shifts time from infra maintenance to product improvements."

- Objection: "How do we know quantized/optimized models won't change outputs?"
  Rebuttal: "We integrate eval-driven regression checks into the rollout pipeline and offer pinned model variants. You can require eval gates before traffic shifts and get per-prompt diffs when drift occurs."

- Objection: "This sounds expensive compared to raw VM hosting."
  Rebuttal: "Raw hosting hides significant engineering costs and operational variance. With Redwood you get predictable reserved pricing, autoscaling policies that avoid overprovision, and batching/caching that lowers effective per-token spend — often cheaper at production scale once you account for developer time and incident costs."

Quick email snippets (one-liners to A/B test):
- To ML engineer: "Tired of drift after you quantize? Try a quick eval-driven rollout demo — see per-prompt diffs before shipping."
- To backend engineer: "Want predictable p95s under heavy burst? 15-minute demo: SDK + canary fallback in practice."
- To platform lead: "Single runtime across hosted/dedicated/private — how we cut cross-team variance and give you reserved-capacity guardrails."

A/B test ideas for copy/landing page sections:
- Emphasize parity-first: headline A: "Same model, same outputs — across clouds and private infra." Headline B: "Predictable inference economics for production LLMs."
- CTA variants: "Run our eval parity check on your model" vs "See a 30-minute reserved-capacity cost projection for your org."

Next steps / recommended follow-ups:
- Build 2 persona-specific sample decks for Solutions Engineering: (1) ML-engineer demo flow, (2) Platform lead procurement checklist.
- Create 3 short video snippets (30–90s) showing eval-to-rollout, SDK fallback behavior, and reserved-capacity dashboard.
- Align with product on a tight one-pager of benchmark numbers we can cite publicly.

Notes & references (internal):
- Internal benchmark deck: confluence:benchmarks/inference-2025-q1
- Eval infra PR: github:infra/eval-pipeline#112
- Pilot customer feedback: JIRA GT-1142 has quotes about "unexpected regressions after quantization"

Author notes / open questions:
- Need to confirm latest p95 numbers with SRE (Liam P. to own).
- Decide if we publish quantization parity guarantees or keep as "best-effort" proof points.

Short checklist for SEs before outreach: 
- Have the customer's current model family and token usage ready.
- Prepare a 15-minute demo focusing on the persona's top metric (eval diffs for ML, p95 timeline for backend, capacity forecast for platform).

End.
